title: Yitzhak Rabin — Born, Raised, And What Came After
description:
Yitzhak Rabin was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. He was the first prime minister to have been born in the region of Palestine, at the time under British control. Rabin was born in Jerusalem to Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe and was raised in a Labor Zionist household.

What Yitzhak Rabin built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. In 1964 he was appointed chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) by Levi Eshkol, who had replaced David Ben-Gurion as Prime Minister and Minister of Defence. Since Eshkol did not have much military experience and trusted Rabin's judgement, he had a very free hand.

scenes.narration: Yitzhak Rabin was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. He was the first prime minister to have been born in the region of Palestine, at the time under British control. Rabin was born in Jerusalem to Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe and was raised in a Labor Zionist household.

To understand where Yitzhak Rabin ended up, start with where Yitzhak Rabin began. As a teenager, he joined the Palmach, the commando force of the Yishuv. He eventually rose through its ranks to become its chief of operations during the 1948 Arab–Israeli War.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Yitzhak Rabin ran through years nobody filmed. In late 1948, he joined the newly formed Israel Defense Forces and continued to rise as a promising officer, with a 27-year career as a professional soldier. He ultimately attained the rank of Rav Aluf, the most senior rank in the Israeli Defense Force (often translated as lieutenant general).

Each stage of the life of Yitzhak Rabin made the next stage possible. In the 1950s, Rabin helped shape the training doctrine of the IDF and he led its Operations Directorate from 1959 to 1963. He was appointed chief of the general staff in 1964 and oversaw Israel's victory in the 1967 Six-Day War.

The people who knew Yitzhak Rabin young describe someone already restless. Rabin served as Israel's ambassador to the United States from 1968 to 1973, during a period of deepening U.S.–Israel ties. In his first term, Rabin signed the Sinai Interim Agreement and ordered the Entebbe raid.

What Yitzhak Rabin built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Rabin was Israel's minister of defense for much of the 1980s, including during the outbreak of the First Intifada. In 1992, Rabin was re-elected as prime minister on a platform embracing the Israeli–Palestinian peace process.

By the time Yitzhak Rabin reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In 1994, Rabin won the Nobel Peace Prize together with long-time political rival Shimon Peres and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat. In November 1995, he was assassinated by Yigal Amir, an extremist who opposed the terms of the Oslo Accords.

The rise of Yitzhak Rabin was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Rabin was the first native-born prime minister of Israel, the only prime minister to be assassinated, and the second to die in office after Levi Eshkol. Nehemiah was born Nehemiah Rubitzov in the shtetl Sydorovychi near Ivankiv in the southern Pale of Settlement (present-day Ukraine).

Setbacks came early for Yitzhak Rabin, and the response to them is the real story. His father Menachem died when he was a boy, and Nehemiah worked to support his family from an early age. At the age of 18, he emigrated to the United States, settling initially in Chicago and then St.

The legacy of Yitzhak Rabin outlived the circumstances that produced it. In 1917, Nehemiah Rabin went to Palestine with a group of volunteers from the Jewish Legion during World War I. Yitzhak's mother, Rosa Cohen, was born in 1890 in Mogilev in Belarus.

Few lives travel as far as that of Yitzhak Rabin, and the distance is the point. Her father, a rabbi, opposed the Zionist movement and sent Rosa to a Christian high school for girls in Gomel, which gave her a broad general education. After working on a kibbutz on the shores of the Sea of Galilee, she moved to Jerusalem.

The childhood of Yitzhak Rabin contains the adult in small print. Nehemiah became a worker for the Palestine Electric Corporation and Rosa was an accountant and local activist. The family moved again in 1931 to a two-room apartment on Hamagid Street in Tel Aviv.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Yitzhak Rabin — in that order. She was among the pioneers of kibbutz Manara from its founding in 1943, and worked as an educator for decades. Yitzhak (Isaac) Rabin grew up in Tel Aviv, where the family relocated when he was one year old.

The turning point in the life of Yitzhak Rabin looked like a failure at the time. He enrolled in the Tel Aviv Beit Hinuch Leyaldei Ovdim (בית חינוך לילדי עובדים, "School House for Workers' Children") in 1928 and completed his studies there in 1935. Rabin mostly received good marks in school, but he was so shy that few people knew he was intelligent.

Every biography of Yitzhak Rabin has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In 1935, Rabin enrolled at an agricultural school on kibbutz Givat Hashlosha that his mother founded. It was here in 1936 at the age of 14 that Rabin joined the Haganah and received his first military training, learning how to use a pistol and stand guard.

The education of Yitzhak Rabin happened mostly outside any school. He excelled in a number of agriculture-related subjects but disliked studying English language—the language of the British "enemy". He originally aspired to be an irrigation engineer, but his interest in military affairs intensified in 1938, when the ongoing Arab revolt worsened.

What Yitzhak Rabin wanted at the start and what Yitzhak Rabin got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. A young Haganah sergeant named Yigal Allon, later a general in the IDF and prominent politician, trained Rabin and others at Kadoorie. For part of 1939, the British closed Kadoorie, and Rabin joined Allon as a security guard at Kibbutz Ginosar until the school re-opened.

The defining trait of Yitzhak Rabin was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. When he finished school, Rabin considered studying irrigation engineering on scholarship at the University of California, Berkeley, although he ultimately decided to stay and fight in Palestine. Leah Rabin was working at the time as a reporter for a Palmach newspaper.

Those who met Yitzhak Rabin at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Similar to the entire Israeli elite of the time, Rabin adhered to a secular-national understanding of Jewish identity, and was non-religious. American diplomat Dennis Ross described him as "the most secular Jew he had met in Israel".

The private years of Yitzhak Rabin explain the public decades better than any speech. In 1941, during his practical training at kibbutz Ramat Yohanan, Rabin joined the newly formed Palmach section of the Haganah, under the influence of Yigal Allon. Rabin could not yet operate a machine gun, drive a car, or ride a motorcycle, but Moshe Dayan accepted the new recruit.

The family Yitzhak Rabin came from matters more than the legends admit. The Palmach was formed as the elite strike force of the Haganah with British assistance as Axis forces approached Palestine. The first operation he participated in was assisting Allied forces in the Syria–Lebanon campaign against Vichy French forces during World War II (the same operation in which Dayan lost his eye) in June–July 1941.

The first real success of Yitzhak Rabin arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Palmach commando units infiltrated Vichy French-held territory and conducted sabotage operations ahead of the main Allied invasion. Rabin was part of a unit that infiltrated Lebanon and conducted telephone sabotage.

The last chapter of Yitzhak Rabin was written long after the fame. As the youngest man in the unit, he was selected to climb the telephone poles and cut the wires. However, as Allied fortunes changed with the Second Battle of El Alamein, the British attempted to dismantle the Palmach.

The whole life of Yitzhak Rabin reads like a single decision repeated. As a Palmachnik, Rabin and his men had to lie low to avoid arousing inquiry from the British administration. After the end of the war the relationship between the Yishuv and the British authorities became strained, especially with respect to the treatment of Jewish immigration.

Between the birth and the legend of Yitzhak Rabin lie the years that actually decide it. In October 1945 Rabin planned a Palmach raid on the Atlit detainee camp in which 208 Jewish illegal immigrants who had been interned there were freed. In 1946, he was arrested in Operation Agatha, a massive British operation against the leaders of the Jewish Establishment in the British Mandate of Palestine and the Palmach known as the "Black Sabbath", and detained for five months.

The reputation of Yitzhak Rabin was built in the middle, not at the edges. After his release he became the commander of the second Palmach battalion and rose to the position of Chief Operations Officer of the Palmach in October 1947. During the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, Rabin directed Israeli operations in Jerusalem and fought the Egyptian army in the Negev.

Somebody like Yitzhak Rabin should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. During the first truce Rabin commanded IDF forces on the beach of Tel Aviv confronting the Irgun during the tragic Altalena Affair. The Altalena ship carried volunteers from abroad coming to fight in War of Independence and large amounts of weapons and ammunition for the war.

The life of Yitzhak Rabin begins far from where the story usually starts. The day after much of the contents were offloaded at Kfar Vitkin the ship was attacked at Ben Gurion's orders off the Tel Aviv shore, set on fire, later  towed out to sea and sunk. Large number of volunteers were killed on board and after jumping in the sea.

In the following period he was the deputy commander of Operation Danny, the largest scale operation to that point, which involved four IDF brigades. The cities of Ramle and Lydda were captured, as well as the major airport in Lydda, as part of the operation.

To understand where Yitzhak Rabin ended up, start with where Yitzhak Rabin began. Following the capture of the two towns there was an expulsion of their Arab population. Later, Rabin was chief of operations for the Southern Front and participated in the major battles ending the fighting there, including Operation Yoav and Operation Horev.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Yitzhak Rabin ran through years nobody filmed. In the beginning of 1949 he was a member of the Israeli delegation to the armistice talks with Egypt that were held on the island of Rhodes. The result of the negotiations were the 1949 Armistice Agreements, which ended the official hostilities of the 1948 Arab–Israeli War.

Each stage of the life of Yitzhak Rabin made the next stage possible. Following the demobilization at the end of the war he was the most senior (former) member of the Palmach that remained in the IDF. Like many Palmach leaders, Rabin was politically aligned with the left wing pro-Soviet Ahdut HaAvoda party and later Mapam.

The people who knew Yitzhak Rabin young describe someone already restless. These officers were distrusted by Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion and several resigned from the army in 1953 after a series of confrontations. Those members of Mapam who remained, such as Rabin, Haim Bar-Lev and David Elazar, had to endure several years in staff or training posts before resuming their careers.

What Yitzhak Rabin built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. In 1964 he was appointed chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) by Levi Eshkol, who had replaced David Ben-Gurion as Prime Minister and Minister of Defence. Since Eshkol did not have much military experience and trusted Rabin's judgement, he had a very free hand.
